solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Spooner's replete, quickly making you grimace

definitions.note: the definition is a participle phrase; the answer is the base verb phrase

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so his name tells you to swap them

parts.note: replete means full up
apace is an old word for at speed
swap the opening F and P sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone who has eaten too much, too fast, ends up wincing.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooner swaps the first sounds: FULL APACE becomes PULL A FACE.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull a face is the everyday idiom for contorting your features in disgust, which is exactly what a grimace is.

clue.text: I would add charitable donations, but no tip, for song

indicators.note: a tip is an end point, so having none means the final letter is cut away

parts.note: a postscript, PS, is what a letter writer adds at the end
alms are gifts to the poor

explanation.surface: A fundraiser adds a plea for donations, but without asking for tips, to a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I would add' reads as a person speaking, but it stands for the postscript a writer tacks on: PS. ALMS loses its last letter to give ALM.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalm is a sacred song or hymn, especially one of those collected in the Bible's Book of Psalms.

clue.text: Maybe sketch process for imposing limits?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a picture made of lines alone, a kind of sketch
second meaning, read the other way round: drawing a line is setting a limit

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reverses the familiar phrase 'drawing the line', which means setting a limit you will not go beyond; the question mark flags the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A sketch done purely in pen strokes is one example of artwork made with lines, hence 'Maybe'; marking boundaries is the punning second sense.

clue.text: Briefly promote theory that's upset old magistrates

indicators.note: in a down clue, to upset something is to tip it over so it reads bottom to top
brief means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to promote a product is to sell it
a theory is an idea

explanation.surface: A short sales pitch for a theory has annoyed some magistrates of old.
explanation.walkthrough: SELL shortened to SEL, then IDEA, and the whole SELIDEA is turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Aediles were officials of ancient Rome responsible for public buildings, games and markets, a kind of magistrate.

clue.text: A case for partnership — part of joint strategy

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell of something, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
a roach is the butt end of a cannabis joint

explanation.surface: A lawyer's case for a business partnership forms one part of a combined strategy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests joint venture to suit 'partnership', but it is a cannabis joint, whose filter end is called the roach.
explanation.definitionFit: An approach is a way of tackling a problem, so it can serve as a synonym for a plan or method.

clue.text: Period crossing desert spelling problems?

indicators.note: one thing crossing another lies across it, so one word straddles the other

parts.note: an era is a period of history
to rat is to desert your side

explanation.surface: A long stretch of time spent crossing a desert brings its own difficulties, as if spelling it out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like a noun, sand and dunes, but it is the verb, and to rat on someone is to desert them. The question mark admits errata cover more than spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are listed printing mistakes in a book, and misspelt words are a typical example of such slips.

clue.text: Crouch, as in the way

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
qua is Latin for 'in the capacity of', that is, as

explanation.surface: Someone squatting down ends up blocking the path.
explanation.walkthrough: Qua is Latin, 'in the capacity of', and is still used in English to mean as; ST is the usual abbreviation for street.
explanation.definitionFit: To squat is to sit on your heels with knees bent, which is the same posture as a crouch.

clue.text: Big cheese to consume gradually on way to work?

parts.note: to sup is to sip a drink slowly
re means on, as in concerning
MO stands for modus operandi, a method of operating

explanation.surface: A boss sipping coffee slowly on the commute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On way to work' paints a commute, but it splits in two: re is the Latin-derived 'concerning', and modus operandi is literally a mode of operating.
explanation.definitionFit: A big cheese is an informal term for an important person in charge, just as a supremo is the overall leader.

clue.text: Raises matter after penny has dropped

indicators.note: a dropped coin falls to the floor, so in this down entry its letter slides from the top to the foot

parts.note: pus is the matter in an infected wound

explanation.surface: A pay rise matters once someone finally understands, when the penny drops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The penny has dropped' is the idiom for understanding, but here P really falls: in PUS it moves from top to bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Ups is a verb meaning increases, as in 'the firm ups its prices', and raises means the same.

clue.text: One rumbling method at heart even more inferior, as it were?

indicators.note: the heart of something is its centre, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the middle two letters of the six-letter word

parts.words: even more inferior, as it were
parts.note: inferior means under, so a made-up comparative gives 'more under'

explanation.surface: A rumbling source whose method is even worse at bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As it were' admits that UNDERER is not a real word: it is a jokey comparative of under. The Thunderer is also a nickname for The Times itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A thunderer is something that booms or rolls loudly, as storm clouds rumble; the Thunderer is also the old nickname for The Times.

clue.text: Spotted hidden camera moving around exhibits

indicators.note: moving around means turning about, so the letters run backwards
to exhibit is to put on show, so the phrase displays the letters within itself

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words, read from the end of the first

explanation.surface: Someone spotted a hidden camera being shifted around in an exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' wants to mean seen, linked to the camera, but it is the adjective meaning pimply. The answer sits backwards inside hidDEN CAmera.
explanation.definitionFit: Acned is a rare adjective for skin marked by acne, that is, covered in pimples or blemishes, so literally spotty.

clue.text: Old men in French city university making even progress

definitions.note: the definition is a participle phrase; the answer is an adverbial Latin phrase meaning at an equal pace

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

parts.note: the capital of France
'old man' is slang for father, and pa is a father
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Elderly men at a Paris university advancing steadily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old men' are not pensioners here: 'the old man' is British slang for one's father, so these are fathers, and they sit inside the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Pari passu is Latin for 'with equal step', used of things that advance side by side at the same rate.

clue.text: What might suggest hero a moderate?

parts.words: What might suggest hero a moderate?
parts.note: surface reading: what would make a hero seem like a moderate person
setter's reading: the letters HERO A are what lies at the centre of the words THE ROAD

explanation.surface: Asking what could make a heroic figure look like a mild centrist.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip the first and last letters from THE ROAD and HERO A is left, the central part of the phrase. That phrase also means politically moderate.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone avoiding extremes in politics or taste is said to take the central path, steering clear of either verge.

clue.text: Show that has eg Paddington Bear number chasing Oscar

indicators.note: to chase is to follow behind, so what follows comes second

parts.note: Oscar is the radio code word for O

indicators.note: to bear is to carry, so one word carries another inside it

parts.note: Paddington is a London railway station
ten is a number

explanation.surface: A show featuring Paddington Bear, with a musical number following an Oscar winner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddington Bear' is the famous storybook bear, but it splits: Paddington is a London railway terminus, and 'Bear' means carry, so the number is carried inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostentation is a showy, pretentious display meant to impress, which is one sense of show as a noun.

clue.text: Bag from overturned kayak finally about to hit the bottom

indicators.note: something overturned is flipped over, so it reads back to front
finally means at the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word
CA, for circa, means about
to spank is to smack someone on the backside

explanation.surface: A bag tumbles from a capsized kayak and is about to sink to the riverbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit the bottom' suggests sinking to the seabed, but it means smacking someone's backside. 'Overturned' applies to the whole string, not just the kayak.
explanation.definitionFit: A knapsack is a soft bag carried on the back, much like a rucksack, so it is a kind of bag.

clue.text: Garish clothing of one found asleep on moor?

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: to kip is to sleep, so a kipper is one who sleeps
to moor a boat is to tie it up

explanation.surface: The loud outfit of a hiker discovered sleeping on open moorland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moor' paints heathland, but it is the verb for tying up a boat. Kip is British slang for sleep, and a kipper is also a smoked herring.
explanation.definitionFit: A kipper tie is a very wide, often brightly patterned necktie fashionable in the 1970s, a classic example of loud dress.

clue.text: With which to sound alarm or ring the changes

indicators.note: changes are alterations, so the letters are reordered into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
a ring is round like the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking which device you would use to raise an alarm or to sound the bells in sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring the changes' is the bell-ringers' phrase for playing every order of the bells; here 'ring' is O and 'changes' shuffles OR, O and THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooter is a siren or horn, the kind of device used to give a loud warning signal in a factory or ship.

clue.text: Good cat food spoiled is a disaster, naturally

indicators.note: spoiled means ruined and gone off, so the letters end up muddled

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
taken as written

explanation.surface: For a cat owner, good cat food going off is a natural catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram needs only one extra letter: G joins the letters of 'cat food'.
explanation.definitionFit: In law and insurance, an act of God is a natural event such as a flood or earthquake that no person could have caused or prevented.

clue.text: Agent's letter from abroad left near

parts.note: phi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
L is the abbreviation for left
by means near, as in 'stand by me'

explanation.surface: A spy's letter sent from overseas has been dropped off nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agent's' reads as possessive, but the 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay. Kim Philby was the British intelligence officer who spied for the Soviet Union.
explanation.definitionFit: Kim Philby was a notorious Cold War double agent in the Cambridge spy ring, so he is a famous example of a secret operative.

clue.text: Howler has been corrected

indicators.note: to correct is to alter and put right, so the letters go into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A schoolboy blunder, a howler, has now been put right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Howler' wants to be a glaring mistake, which suits 'corrected', but it is a creature that wails.
explanation.definitionFit: In Irish folklore a banshee is a female spirit whose wailing cry foretells a death, a literal howler.

clue.text: Chestnut placed in rather large glass

indicators.note: what is placed in something ends up inside it

parts.note: 'I'd rather' and 'I'd sooner' mean the same
CH is the abbreviation for chestnut, the horse colour

explanation.surface: A chestnut dropped into a fairly big glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rather large' reads as one phrase meaning quite big, but 'rather' is wordplay and 'large glass' the definition. CH is used for chestnut in horse-racing form.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is a tall glass for sherry or, in Australia, beer, larger than a standard small glass.

clue.text: Blunder that hurts knight meeting end

parts.note: ow is what you say when something hurts
N is the chess notation for a knight
a goal is an end you aim for

explanation.surface: A painful mistake that sees a knight meet his death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunder that hurts' looks like the whole definition, but 'that hurts' is the cry OW.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoring into your own net in football is the literal sense; figuratively it is any action that backfires on the person who did it.

clue.text: Text message's recipient is certainly one taking abnormal interest

parts.note: U is text-speak for you, the person a message is sent to
'sure' is a casual way of saying certainly
R is text-speak for are, the plural form of is

explanation.surface: Whoever gets the text message is clearly nosy, showing unusual interest.
explanation.walkthrough: In text-speak 'U SURE R' means 'you sure are': the recipient certainly is. 'Interest' is not curiosity but money charged on a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at excessive rates, so the extra charged is interest beyond the normal or lawful level.

clue.text: Anger once as dog close to group disrupted kids' event

indicators.note: something disrupted is thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dog's past bad temper near the group spoiled the children's sports day.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a story about an angry dog, but all fourteen letters of the first four words, plus P, are the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg-and-spoon race is a traditional school sports day contest where children run balancing an egg on a spoon.

clue.text: Figure in veil: it is seen on and off

indicators.note: something seen on and off flickers in and out of view, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters spell a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A shape glimpsed through a veil, appearing and vanishing.
explanation.walkthrough: The kept letters V, I, I, I spell VIII, the Roman numeral for the answer, so you must translate them before writing in.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight is a number, and figure is a common crossword synonym for any numeral or digit.

clue.text: What follows this pill potentially is safer to swallow?

definitions.text: What follows this pill potentially is safer to swallow?

parts.words: What follows this pill potentially is safer to swallow?
parts.note: surface reading: a medical question about a tablet that makes the next dose easier to take
setter's reading: what follows is what the patient says next, which is honest, and plain fact is proverbially hard to swallow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallow' suggests taking medicine, but it is the idiom for accepting something hard to believe. After this pill, what the taker says is honest, though perhaps not easy to accept.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug such as sodium pentothal is supposed to make a captive speak candidly, so whatever comes out afterwards is believed reliable.

clue.text: Bath for one boy not in total agreement

indicators.note: something not in is left out, so those letters are removed

parts.note: in unison means in complete agreement
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A bath for one boy who doesn't fully agree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bath for one' looks like a single tub, but it is the English city, home of the University of Bath. UNISON loses SON.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath has a well-known university, so it is one example of a uni, the informal British term for a university.

clue.text: Outstanding, timeless drag act

indicators.note: timeless means without time, and T, for time, is the letter taken out

parts.note: towing is the act of dragging something behind a vehicle

explanation.surface: An excellent drag show that never dates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drag act' suggests a cross-dressing performance, but it is the act of dragging: TOWING, minus T for time.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt that is outstanding has not yet been paid, which is what owing means when said of money.

clue.text: Cream containing energy: good for slimmers?

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for energy
lite is the food-label spelling for low in calories

explanation.surface: Asking whether a cream full of energy can suit people on a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cream' suggests the dairy product, which fits slimmers, but it means the best of a group.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of a group is its finest members, and the elite are the select top tier of any society.

clue.text: Otherworldly appearance of padre involved with Lent

indicators.note: something involved is tangled up, so the letters are mixed together

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chaplain caught up in Lent has an unearthly look about him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the two parts of the anagram material. 'Otherworldly appearance' suggests a ghostly look; it is a world other than ours as it appears in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars is called this because of its rusty colour as seen from Earth, so it is another world's visible look.
